speechtext: It applies to both; it must be aged at least four years.

I notice that by a departmental ordinance or decree of the United States liquor imported in bottles cannot bear a label containing the words "bottled in bond under government supervision," and I understand that it has been determined in the United States that these words cannot be used on bottled goods imported even though it is stated on the label that these goods are bottled in Canada and not in the United States. It has been called to my attention that the application of this departmental ordinance or decree will practically preclude the export of bottled goods which have been bottled in bond under government supervision in Canada. If that is correct it will certainly restrict to a very considerable degree the value of this item 802. Perhaps later the minister will deal with the question. This ordinance or decree, according to its terms, was to come into force on February 15 last, but I understand that, by reason of the negotiation of the Canada-United States trade agreement which is now under the consideration of this committee, its application was postponed for six months. I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that unless that matter is determined now I can foresee that once this agreement is ratified by parliament there will be little chance indeed of having that ordinance repealed, and I bring to his attention the fact that the effect of that ordinance will be to destroy the industry engaged in bottling liquors in Canada and tend to transfer that bottling industry to the United States. I am simply calling attention to this as a factor which mitigates against Canadian exporters receiving the full advantage of the agreement.
There is another matter to which I would call attention. In a bill which has already passed the house of representatives and is now under the consideration of the senate of the United States, section 403a provides as follows:
Whenever the Secretary of the Treasury finds that there has been instituted, or that process has been issued for the institution of, any proceeding by the United States, based upon a claim arising under the customs or internal revenue laws in connection with an alleged importation or bringing into the United States of distilled spirits, wines, or fermented malt
liquors, against any person, whether or not a resident of the United States, and that such person has, or at the date of the enactment of this act had, a substantial interest, direct or indirect, in any plant, establishment, or business outside of the United States for the production, manufacture, rectification, selling, or marketing of distilled spirits, wines, or fermented malt liquors, the secretary shall publish such information as will, in his judgment, sufficiently identify such person and such plant, establishment, or business, and after such publication no distilled spirits, wines, or fermented malt liquors produced, manufactured, rectified, sold or marketed by such person, or in which he has any interest, or produced, manufactured, rectified, sold or marketed in or by any such plant, establishment, or business shall be imported or brought into the United States unless and until such person submits to the jurisdiction of the court of the United States in which such proceeding has been instituted, or out of which such process has been issued, and, to secure payment of the claim, furnishes to the Secretary of the Treasury such security as he may require, but not in excess of double the amount of the claim, or complies with such other reasonable terms as he may impose.
It is well known-and I do not wish to enter into a detailed discussion of it-that the United States treasury has preferred claims either directly or indirectly against almost every leading Canadian distillery and is seeking to impose penalties and obtain payment of a vast number of claims amounting to many tens of millions of dollars from Canadians who are domiciled and resident in this country, and who are not subject to the jurisdiction of United States courts. This bill, which appears to me to attempt by an indirect method to obtain jurisdiction over Canadian nationals domiciled in Canada and over whom the United States courts would not, except for this proposed enactment, obtain jurisdiction, is one which, if enacted by the Congress of the United States, would really reduce almost to a nullity the advantages of the reduction proposed to be made in this agreement from $5 customs duty per gallon to S2.50 per gallon on Canadian whiskey entering the United States.
I do not know that I have ever drunk a glass of Canadian whiskey in my life and therefore I am not personally interested-
What are you waiting for?

Well, I can find other decoctions which suit my taste better. But I commend this item and this proposed reduction, not from the point of view of the whiskey trade, but because it is one item in this agreement which will, I think, to a certain extent enable Canada to reduce the balance of trade which now and for many years has been against us in our dealings with

the United States. I discussed that question once, and I am simply referring to it for this moment again. I am thoroughly convinced we cannot maintain any stable monetary policy in this country so long as we are purchasing from the United States, as we have done in years past, so many million dollars in value of their products in excess of the value of the products which we sell to them. I think that goes to the very root of our monetary and credit policy. From that point of view I commend this item to the committee and intend to vote for it, and I would do anything I reasonably could to secure its approval by the committee. But with that I have in my mind that, if the bill which, having already passed the house of representatives, is now before the United States senate, is enacted and enforced in the United States, it will almost completely wipe out any advantage which we would otherwise obtain under this item of the proposed agreement now under consideration. I would like to be assured by the government that every reasonable measure is being taken to represent to the United States government, and through that government to the United States congress, that the enactment of the bill now under consideration in the United States senate would preclude this country taking any reasonable advantage of the item.
I do not wish to cast any aspersions, but I remember in my youthful days, under an old reciprocity agreement of many years ago, preserved fish was permitted to enter the United States free of duty, and that was followed by a United States duty on the tin cans which absolutely precluded us from doing business in that country by the export of those fish products in proper packages. I trust that, concealed beneath this item, there is not the prospective enactment of the section of the bill to which I have called attention and which was discussed and passed by the house of representatives on August 22, 1935, the whole bill being found at page 14120 of the congressional record for that date.

Perhaps I might point out to my hon. friend that there is an article in the agreement, Article XI, which is intended to meet the sort of contingency that he and possibly others may have in mind. Article XI reads:
In the event that the government of either country adopts any measure which, even though it does not conflict with the terms of this agreement, is considered by the government of the other country to have the effect of nullifying or impairing any object of the agreement, the government which has adopted any such measure shall consider such representations and proposals as the other government may make with a view to effecting a mutually satisfactory adjustment of the matter.
That provision has been inserted to avoid the possibility of occurrences of the kind my hon. friend has mentioned. Of course, as the minister has just said, it is not within the province of one country to interfere in the domestic affairs of another country, and it is not for the government of Canada to tell either the house of representatives or the senate of the United States what they should or should not do. Nothing of that kind could appear in any agreement; it would not be permitted to appear. But I can assure my hon. friend that with respect to this matter, as far as it affects Canadian interests, the position and the interests of Canada have been most fully represented at Washington, I have every reason to believe that such representations are being sympathetically considered, though what final action may be taken by any legislative body in the United States it is, of course impossible to say.

I am glad to hear what the Prime Minister has just said on this subject. I only want to ask now, since I understand that there is in the agreement a provision for negotiation if a clause of the agreement is completely nullified by some other legislation, whether in case such negotiations should not be successful that would give Canada the right to terminate the agreement. very substantially reduced, from 15 to 10 per cent. That is an accomplished fact under the agreement.

That is the tendency that prevails throughout this whole agreement, namely, for the United States to take our raw products free or at reduced rate, to have them worked up by American labour, and then shipped into this country in the form of finished articles, incorporating American labour and giving business to American people instead of to Canadian.

It is doubtful whether some of the articles mentioned by my hon. friend could be shipped into the United States from Canada if there were no tariff at all. These goods probably enter the United States from European countries or Japan, and they enter the United States now over a high tariff wall.

But we shall never be in a position to export them to the United States so long as we encourage mass production in that country and leave our smaller producers under the disadvantages that prevail throughout this whole agreement.
Is the hon. member objecting to selling things in the United States or anywhere else?

Certainly not, but I object to the United States incorporating 65 per cent of American labour into the raw products which we ship over there and then sending them back as finished products over here, but that is the tendency of this treaty from beginning to end. In only a very few cases do we get the 50 per cent reduction which the president could have given us, but in very many cases we give a reduction of more than 50 per cent, and make some items free altogether, and then this government wants the Canadian people to think that they are getting great advantages by shipping our raw products to the United States, while actually this agreement is closing our factories by giving an increased advantage to the United States on the finished product.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let me just follow what my hon. friend has said. First of all he says that we send our raw' products to the United States. He admits that there is a duty on these products going into the United States. He will admit that any of the
products which we are here discussing which go into the United States under this agreement will still pay a duty, because the president had authority to reduce the existing duty by only 50 per cent. He says that after our raw products have gone into the United States, paid the duty, and the Americans have manufactured them into finished articles they have then shipped them back into Canada. But the manufactured articles on coming back here would have to be subject to the intolerably high tariffs which hon. gentlemen opposite have imposed in the last few years. He then says that after the finished articles from the United States have met the high Canadian tariff, they undersell the products of our Canadian manufactures. Well, there could not be a stronger argument for the necessity of some tariff changes which will serve to bring about competition with what in the circumstances must be combines in this country which are holding up prices to an exorbitant figure against the consumer.

Mr. Chairman, I have every respect for the Prime Minister's splendid arguments but I certainly have not much regard for the type of argument that puts words into my mouth that I did not use. While the Prime Minister rarely gets absolutely crossways he certainly in this case has put absolutely the opposite construction on my argument to what it bears. The duties I was complaining against were the United States duties on our similar finished products entering that countiy. Certainly we have no high tariffs on the highly processed commodities entering Canada under this item, or under any other item in this agreement. Look down the list and you will find the same thing all through. I mentioned finished articles such as ladies' purses and gentlemen's club bags on which the United States charges us a duty of 50 per cent, or half the value, when we attempt to send these goods into that country, but we can send our hides and our cattle over there free or at a very small rate of duty, and they will take those hides and put American labour to work on them. They will take our partly finished leather, it is true, and this item reduces the duty from 12 to 10 per cent. They will take our semifinished products at a 10 per cent rate, but when the article is finished by Canadian labour they charge us 50 per cent under this agreement. What we are saying to the United States in this agreement is this: We appreciate very much your taking our raw hides and our calf skins and so forth at a reduced tariff duty so that you may finish them by American labour, and then we will let you send them
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

back to Canada at a reduction of about 50 per cent in the duty, while our similar finished goods get no reduced rate at all going into the United States. Surely the Prime Minister would not argue that that was any advantage to Canadian labour. May I remind him again, and emphasize that this agreement is favouring American labour and American factories all down the line.
As a farmer I admit that it is in some instances some slight help to us when there is a temporary market in the United States, and when they are not destroying their cattle we can get a slight advantage, although it has always been a question just what that advantage amounts to. But so far as Canadian labour is concerned, in my province of Ontario and your province of Quebec, Mr. Chairman (Sir Eugene Fiset), thousands and thousands of men are idle to-day, and I warn the government again that the whole principle of this agreement is prejudicing the chances of Canadian workmen getting or keeping a job. In 1930, when our workmen lost their jobs through the tariff tinkering of the government that was in office before 1930, about 495,000 of them found employment in the United States, but now their employment there has ended and they are coming back to Canada, where thousands of Canadian boys have already lost their jobs since this agreement came into effect, and unlike the years before 1930 they cannot now find jobs in the United States, so the situation is entirely different. This government has hurt their chances of finding employment in Canada, and world conditions have contributed to eliminating their chances of finding work in foreign factories, a chance which was open to them when this government was in power before. The whole tendency of the agreement is to send our raw materials to the United States to be finished. This employs American labour; it takes a certain number from the relief camps of the United States, but it adds to the number in the relief camps in Canada.

speechtext: That is the result of my hon. friend's argument; that is the logic of his remarks. My hon. friend says that the whole purpose of this agreement is the sending of commodities one way only. May I say to him that the purpose of this agreement is to promote trade. My hon. friend is ready to promote only one kind of trade. He does not take the view that trade will not exist unless it is beneficial to both parties. Those who sell raw materials to the United States are selling them because it pays them to do so. Those who buy finished articles from the United States do so because they are getting what they want for their money. They are getting more than they would get if they were compelled to buy in a restricted market here. Trade is an exchange of commodities but my hon. friend treats it all as economic warfare. If trade is a mutually beneficial exchange of commodities, the more of it we have the better it will be for all on both sides of the line.

I am delighted
to find out that the Prime Minister and I stand on common ground in connection with at least one thing. I have always had great admiration for the genial attitude of my right hon. friend, much more than I have had for his political soundness. I want to make it clear to the committee, and par-

trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Goods will not come from any front into this country unless they are serving someone's use and benefit. If our farmers can purchase their agricultural implements abroad more cheaply than they otherwise could, instead of purchasing them from some monopolistic group, they will be able to sell their products more advantageously in the markets of the world and thus secure more purchasing power in the home market with consequent benefit to Canadian manufacturers.

I may be able to give a little comfort to those on the other side who are alarmed with regard to the balance on the sale and purchase of agricultural implements, because as a matter of fact the balance of increase is in our favour. In the month of January, 1936, exports of farm implements to the United States were $192,000 greater than in the same month of the previous year, and here is the point. Imports of farm implements into Canada from the United States were greater by $145,000 in January, 1936,

than in the same month of the previous year. So that there was a net gain to the Canadian implement industry in January, 1936, over January, 1935, of $47,000; and in February exports also increased; last year $73,000 worth and this year, February, $209,000 worth. So that there is nothing to be particularly alarmed about.

I do not think that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) is alarmed about the duty. I think what be and his associates are thinking of is that this is not a real reciprocity; that the agreements are "using us too good"; that the United States are letting our implements in free and we should let their agricultural implements in free also in order to make a real reciprocity. I think they are kicking about the duty they have on their agricultural implements, and the only way to satisfy them is to take the duty off agricultural implements coming into Canada and make it real reciprocity.
I think the hon. member who has just spoken is really advocating a higher price for agricultural implements. What happened when the duty was taken off?

The price of agricultural implements in this country dropped while the Liberal party was in power, regardless of what my hon. friends say. The price of agricultural implements rose from 1911 until 1920.
What about 1921 to 1930?

Then, after the Liberal party came into power, the price of agricultural implements dropped from the price they were in 1921. The only thing that happened to agricultural implements while my hon. friends were in power from 1930 to 1935 was that they stayed at the same price to which they had been lowered from 1921 to 1930. Look it up and you will find that I am correct.

I do not wish to
hold up this item; I do not oppose the item "Free," and I quite appreciate that we get our manufactured goods into the United States free. But on the point that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has mentioned, I regret to have to say that I believe he is absolutely incorrect. I have made a careful study of the prices of farm implements on three or four occasions; I have placed it on Hansard in this parliament, and I stand by the records of Hansard. I stand by what I

said because I studied it carefully, checked and double-checked it. It is true, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw says, that prices went up between 1911 and 1921, but everyone in this house will agree that it is unfair to charge the Conservative party with what was a world war condition. The price of western wheat went up to about S3 a bushel before it was controlled. It is absolutely unfair therefore to say that the increase in prices during those years was due to the Conservative party. Prices of farm implements, like prices of everything else, went up from 1911 to 1921, but may I point out that in 1911 we were producing in Canada-and I wish the Prime Minister would listen to this as well-seventy per cent of our total consumption of farm implements and we were providing the world with enormous quantities of agricultural implements as well. We had in 1911 a flourishing agricultural implement industry. I know that every member will realize that after 1921, when the present government were in power before, when the duty was lowered, the price of farm implements did not go down; it went up. I wish to say to the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly)-
Look it up.

I have looked it
up on scores of occasions; I advise you to look it up. I know that neither the hon. member for Moose Jaw nor the hon. member for Wood Mountain wishes to misrepresent facts. We were at the time the Prime Minister made the statement.

No, the right hon. gentleman was answering the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and he asked if as farmers we still wished to pay for the monopolistic control of farm implements. I say that to-day we are producing only a portion of our consumption of farm implements. Our exports are not as great, but I think we are producing only about thirty-five per cent of our consumption instead of about seventy per cent, which was the case before the tariffs were lowered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I suggest to my hon. friend that the points to which is is referring now, particularly the facts, will be developed before a committee of this house. Then the hon. gentleman will be relieved of the necessity of saying "I think" so and so, because the actual facts can be made a matter of record,
A rather important aspect of this matter was touched upon by the hon. member for Davenport, who is always concerned, much to his credit, with the effect of what we are doing upon the fortunes of workingmen and upon the volume of industry in this country. I think if he studies the agricultural implement industry he will find that during the period when the maximum importations into Canada took place our own implement industry was busier than at any other period; in fact our greatest exports of these commodities coincide, curiously enough, with very large imports and with maximum production at home. There are reasons for all these things which do not necessarily relate to tariffs, and neither is it true that putting up or putting down the tariff on agricultural implements by a few points necessarily puts workmen out of
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

work or into work. Obviously if it were possible to put men to work by increasing the tariff on agricultural implements the record of the employment during the past five years should not have been what it was, because everyone knows that there has been a steady and continuous decline in employment in the agricultural implement industry under the high tariffs imposed by my hon. friends opposite in 1931.
Due to the depression.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is only now that we are seeing a slight improvement in the agricultural implement industry and in the volume of work available to Canadian workingmen. I think we should not make the mistake of assuming that changing the tariff by a few points materially affects employment. Certainly the large tariff increases brought about by my hon. friends opposite when they were in office did not increase Canadian employment in that industry.

I have been interrupted quite a number of times from both sides of the house, though I was not nearly finished. However, I am not now going to detain the committee more than a moment or two. I should like to say a word to the Minister of Finance. I know he wants to be fair, and I know he has had a good deal of business experience, but from what he said I inferred that he believed the substantial duties on agricultural implements brought in by the late government were responsible for the decreased production in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.
That was the impression I obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I said the duties imposed by my hon. friends opposite certainly did not increase Canadian employment in that industry.

I will say this, that the duties imposed by the late government did increase employment in the agricultural implement industry as compared with what would have been the case if the duties had not been increased.
How do you know that?

I know that from my business experience. That is a fact, and I know the minister is big enough to admit that but it would not be good politics for him to do so. Now I should like to say just a word further. Did I understand the minister to say that Canada is now exporting to 
the United States more agricultural implements than she is buying from the United States?
No, I said the exports were increasing more rapidly than the imports.

I am very glad to hear that, but I had the impression that the minister said we were selling more to the United States than we were buying from them. I noticed that in 1934-35, the last year for which I have the figures, we exported to the United States $300,000 worth of implements and imported from that country
82,000,000 worth. Then just one more word in reference to what the Prime Minister said in regard to a brick for a brick. In this case it is not a brick for a brick; it is seven bricks against the Canadian worker to one brick against the United States worker.
How do you know?

In 1931 we imported
from the United States $15,000,000 worth of agricultural implements while we shipped them $2,000,000 worth. That is seven to one, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That is a small concession.

I have been tempted

I have sat in my place and listened to longer speeches about farm implements made by hon. members opposite within the last few days.

Anyway, they were objected to, and in this instance I must certainly call for a decision from the chair. If we are to enter into a general debate other speeches will follow, and we will not complete the discussion on the agreement before many days. We are discussing an item respecting agricultural implements, and I believe the minister is simply answering some questions asked by other hon. members.
There is no item concerning imports of agricultural implements under discussion.
Yes.

As a result of the change of government on December 31, 1921, there was a change of government policy respecting farm implements. I have before me a list of prices for the present year. Did not the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen lower the tariff around or before 1921?

There certainly

My friend says there

Or how the price of a cultivator got down from $126 to $113 if there was no reduction in the price? Or how the price of a wagon got down from $217 to $128? So we have that level of prices maintained which was put into effect, not by the

Let me go a little further. They say in this article that if you are not satisfied to run your farm with horse-drawn implements but want a tractor, you would have had to pay for that tractor in 1914, with tariffs as they were then, 82,350, but with the reductions that were made on tractors by Mr. Meighen during the time he was in power the price went down from 52,350 to $2,100, again indicating that even when a Conservative government lowers tariffs the price goes down. But what has happened since then? From 1921 down to 1936 the reduction for the same tractor has been from $2,100 in 1921 to $1,079 in 1936, under the lower tariffs that were put into effect.
For the same type of tractor?

It is the same type of tractor right across for the three years, a 15-30 horsepower tractor. A 22-inch thresher cost 81,175 in 1914 and $1,645 in 1921, and costs $1,179 in 1936. So if you want to operate your farm with a tractor and have a thresher it would cost you for this list of implements that I have given, $4,601.50 in 1914, $5,784.50 in 1921, and $3,856.75 in 1936. a reduction of practically $2,000 in the cost of equipping your farm for threshing and putting in and harvesting the crop, a reduction of about $2,000 in equipping your farm with the necessary machinery under low tariff policies as compared with the higher price under the high tariff policies of previous years.
They go on to make a further comparison. The increase in the price of implements from 1914 to 1921 was 89 per cent. The decrease in the price from 1921 to 1936 was 22 per cent. Including a 15-30 horsepower tractor and a 22-inch thresher in the equipment, the increase in price from 1914 to 1921 was 23 per cent. The decrease in price from 1921 to 1936 is 33$ per cent. The decrease in price from 1914 to 1936 is 16 per cent.

Does the minister
attribute that difference in price entirely to tariffs? Is not some of it attributable to the cheapness with which tractors can be produced in recent years?

I think I said at the beginning of my remarks that I did not attribute all of that increase in price to tariffs, nor do I attribute all of the decrease in the other case to tariffs. But I d'o say this, that apart altogether from the direct influence of the tariff itself on prices, the change in conditions, the increase in prices all along the line, brought about by high tariffs increasing the price of everything along with the particular articles affected, naturally had its effect on the price of farm implements. The point I was going to make in connection with the comparisons I have made, and the fact I want to emphasize, is that tariffs do have an effect upon prices. You will notice that when you leave the tractor out of consideration, on which the duty was lowered in both periods, you get a different result. For example, taking the implements upon which tariffs were maintained high all the way through the period, the cost of the implements almost doubled.
In connection with tractors, there was a reduction in the tariff and there was also a total reduction in prices amounting to $250,000 during that same period. A moment ago my hon. friend tried to create the impression that the main reason for the increases in prices during that period was the war. This should have applied to tractors as well as to other implements, but in spite of the war the price of tractors was reduced while prices of other implements went up. This increase was due to war conditions and the conditions which obtained immediately following the war. Apparently the reduction in the duty on tractors had the effect of overcoming these other conditions and bringing about a reduction in prices. It has been said day after day in this committee that tariffs have no effect upon prices, either to put them up or to bring them down, that the effect has been opposite to that indicated by hon. members on this side, but these contentions are not borne out by the figures presented by the implement industry.

I rise
again to speak to this matter, not just because it is of great interest to the constituency which I have the honour to represent, but because I believe it is of grave concern to the whole dominion. It has been said time and time again, both in this chamber and throughout the country, that unemployment is Canada's greatest problem. In discussing all matters I believe we should bear this in mind. The Minister of Finance has stated that from 1921 to 1930 occurred the greatest production of farm implements in Canada, and also the greatest exportation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And imports also.

And imports also. To what countries were we exporting? We were not exporting to the United States; we were exporting to Europe
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

and other foreign countries. To-day conditions have changed entirely. We should not compare conditions as they exist to-day with those that existed in 1921 or 1925. We cannot go back to the old horse and buggy days when transportation was so slow and when a blacksmith was situated on every corner. We cannot all be Rip Van Winkles; we must wake up and realize that because of changed economic conditions we must do business on a different basis. From 1921 to 1930 the markets of Europe and other foreign countries were open to Canada, but to-day those markets are practically all closed. During the period from 1921 to 1930 our implement manufacturers were exporting to France, Germany, Russia, Australia and other countries which I could name, but to-day it is practically impossible to ship any implements to those countries.
The agricultural implement manufacturing industry is very important and one which should be preserved for the workingmen of this country, but in preserving this industry we must not act unfairly to any class of people. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has shown that to-day prices of farm implements are no higher than they were in 1925. He referred to the great drop which had occurred since 1921 in the price of tractors, but I would direct his attention to the fact that that drop was due to a change in methods of production. I think the minister stated himself that the drop in prices was not due to the tariff. A change occurred in methods of production of tractors just as it did in methods of production of automobiles. Prior to that time automobiles were manufactured by many small companies; the days of mass production had not arrived. The same applied to the manufacture of tractors. When a change in the methods occurred, prices dropped.
My point is that if unemployment is one of Canada's greatest problems, the agricultural implement industry should be preserved to this country on a fair basis. The other day an hon. member opposite referred to conditions which had existed in this industry from 1930 to 1936 because of high tariffs. I do not think anyone should take any credit for the conditions that existed in this industry during that period. That industry had practically closed up, but now the factories are running. If we can supply implements to the fanners at a fair price we shall be acting fairly to the farmer and to the manufacturer; we shall be acting fairly to the investor and to the great mass of working people who earn their living in these factories.

Could the hon. member
give me the exports of agricultural implements from Canada during 1934?
Mr. MACDONALD (Brantford); I have not the figures, but I am sure that by 1934 exports of agricultural implements had reached a very low level indeed. Exports were very low and there cannot be any increase because of the high tariffs which have been put up against Canadian implements.

I should like to place
some figures on Hansard. In 1934 the production of farm implements and machinery was valued at $8,817,000; imports were valued at $3,204,000 and exports at $3,351,000. That shows that there must have been some exports. In 1924 the production was valued at $24,770,000 and imports at $6,585,000. I ask hon. members to notice that figure and work out the percentage of imports to production in 1924 and 1934. In 1924 exports were valued at $11,356,000.

In
1924 there were no tariffs against us.

I want the hon. member to figure out the relationship of production to exports and imports during that year. Notwithstanding the tariff barriers raised against implements coming into this country, in 1934 the percentage of imports to production was higher than it was in 1924. So far as I am concerned and so far as the Liberal party is concerned, we were elected on a platform of reduced tariffs.

I did not expect to enter
into this discussion, but after listening to many of our friends in the opposition I think I ought to say something, speaking as a farmer who represents that excellent constituency of Brant, which circles around the agricultural implement industry of Brantford. Brantford is known as a community that produces agricultural implements, and I have the honour to represent a riding in which there is one of these implement manufacturers. I assure you therefore that I am interested in the general wellbeing of the city of Brantford and in the welfare of the people employed in these industries. After all the prosperity of the labouring man in Brantford is dependent on these industries and the manner in which they are prepared to function and to sell their products to the farmers; but it is also dependent upon the ability of the farmers to buy the products of the factories, and the ability of the farmers to do that is in turn dependent upon their purchasing power. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) made a remark which suggested to me that

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
the discussion of the question of agricultural implements in regard to prices is actually not fair from the standpoint of the general welfare and prosperity of the people employed in these factories. He said he did not wish to question the remarks of some hon. gentlemen because he knew they wanted to be honest. I have not known my hon. friend personally long enough to wish to attempt to defend his integrity-

You do not need
to.

-but I would refer to a
statement made by the hon. gentleman in connection with prices. In 1914 you could buy a binder costing S165 for 170 bushels of wheat; to-day you have to pay 320 bushels of wheat. Now the price of any commodity depends upon the exchange of services. I come from a mixed farming section; the dairy industry enters to a large extent into our labours up there. In 1914 I had to give 555 pounds of butter for that same binder, whereas in 1936 I have to give 1,024 pounds of butter for it. I ask you in all fairness to the farmers, who are the customers of the men engaged in the agricultural implement industries: Is there not a great relationship between the general prosperity of the farmers buying those products and the prices which the farmers themselves receive for the commodities they have to sell? I take the view that the salvation, the road to recovery, is in the reducing of the cost of commodities to the consumer. You increase the purchasing power of every man, woman and child the moment you do that, because every one of us is a consumer. I am prepared to take issue with my colleague, who is absolutely sincere, in this. The salvation of the labouring man in the city of Brantford is in his ability to make more machinery to sell to the customers of the manufacturers, that is to say, the farmers, whose purchasing power must be increased if they are to buy more implements and thereby keep more men employed in the factories. We 'have to save the implement manufacturers from themselves.

Leave out the word
implement.

I would gladly do that and
just say manufacturers. There is an implement manufacturing concern in my constituency, the Cockshutt Plow Company. I am very proud of that concern and it has made a splendid contribution to the progress of the community, so that I do not want to see anything happen to those works. There are many labouring men adjacent to Brantford who want work in the Cockshutt factory, and 12739-79
I feel that the solution of their problems lies in their ability to produce more implements so that more employment can be afforded these men. But I cannot see any other way of accomplishing this than to bring about a condition of affairs in which there will be a lower cost of production resulting in increased purchasing power to the farmers and other consumers so that there will be a greater distribution of the human satisfaction of life in various commodities.
We have heard a great deal about the home market. The national policy was supposed to be instituted for the benefit of the home market, in the interests of the farmers. I am prepared to hand it back to the protectionists. I say that the home market for our industrial centres lies in the ability of the farmers to purchase the commodities they need and in an increase in the purchasing power of consumers at large, so that the farmers may have an opportunity to buy more of the things which are enjoyed in the privileged cities.

I did not intend saying anything on this implement item, because there is a committee, to which reference has been made, to which we might have looked for the figures. Possibly that would have been more or less the proper place in which to obtain a good many of the figures that have been put on the record this afternoon. I do not think there is any member who has purchased more agricultural implements than I have in the last twenty-five years. I have sat on most of the machines mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture and I know just how some of them run, how easily they operate. And I know that when you compare the 1914 implement with the implement of 1929 or 1936 you are comparing altogether different things. You cannot make a fair comparison of prices because the later machine is altogether different.

How then does the hon. gentleman answer the question asked a few moments ago by one of the members from Alberta, when he implied that the price of a tractor went down as you improved the tractor? Why should other prices go up as you improve other implements?

It is a matter of mass production. The Minister of Finance made a statement with which I agree and which I think was very interesting. He said that production was greatest during the years when our imports from the United States were greatest, and that is fair. But there was a reason for that; it was on account

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

of the demand. From 1917 to 1930 there was in western Canada a period in which there was a great demand for agricultural implements, following the war, when a greater production scheme was in progress. The farmers had not purchased many implements during the war, and in the subsequent period there was a great demand. Production demanded more implements and certainly there was the demand. That was what created it.
The figures quoted by the Minister of Agriculture are very interesting and no doubt are correct, but I should like to quote prices for two or three years during which hon. gentlemen opposite were in power-1923 and 1924. I have here a list of implements provided by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, internal trade branch, retail prices of specified agricultural implements, 1913-34. I know there was an increase in the prices of certain implements-I have the lines here-from 1923 to 1924. For instance, walking ploughs, which in 1923 were $33.25, increased to $36.40. The double disc drill increased from $243 to $276. I am going to give the price in 1934, which will give you an indication that there has been a reduction in the price during the last four years. The double disc drill I have just quoted, from $243 in 1923 to $276 in 1924, was $240 in 1934. Hay rakes, $56.50 in 1923, increased to $66 in 1924-just one year. In 1934 the hay rake was $57.50. In 1923 an eight foot binder was $288, and in 1924, $313. I may say that 1924 was the peak year of prices of agricultural implements in Canada.
Just before the tariff was cut on agricultural implements.
Just before it was cut? I may say that the tariff was cut considerably in 1921. That was the lowest tariff we had had, I think, on agricultural implements.
No.

In 1934 that binder was $266. The mower, quoted by the Minister of Agriculture, in 1923 was $99; in 1924, $111; in 1934, $94. The disc harrow in 1923 was $73.50; in 1924, $83.50; in 1934, $72.25. The gang plough in 1923 was $158.75, and in 1924, $170.50; 1934, $138. The wagon, which in 1923 was $187, increased to $195 in the one year, and in 1934 it was $170.75.
Figures can be quoted to make a misrepresentation of the actual facts. The list quoted by the Minister of Agriculture, I think, is not a fair indication. He takes 1914, compares it with 1921, and then 1936; I think 1935 should have been included to show what the price was

last year, and then you will see that there has been an increase this year. I am just as anxious as any member of this house to see cheaper implements. The important thing is how to get them. As I said before, this item is free, and I do not see much purpose in discussing it. The matter is really before the committee that has been set up, and I think that a lot of this discussion is practically out of order.

The difference in the range of prices, in both the west and the east, substantiates the statements that I placed on record on many occasions to the effect that prices rose from 1921 to 1930. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) has shown that they rose in western Canada from 1921 to 1930; they certainly rose in eastern Canada, and despite what any hon. member may wish to place on Hansard there can be no doubt as to the prices at points such as Toronto, Brantford, Montreal and all points east. I might point out also, without delaying the committee too long, that during these years the duty was reduced from 12J per cent to 6J or 6 per cent. Hon. members will also recall that Hon. W. S. Fielding reduced the sales tax on farm implements by, I think it was, 5 per cent. The reduction of the duty on the price of a binder meant, at the 1921 price, about $15, and the reduction of the sales tax meant about $13.30. Together the reduction of the tariff and the reduction of the sales tax represented about $28 reduction on that implement. We were told by the government of that day and its supporters that we farmers could expect a reduction of approximately $28 on the price of a binder. What was the result? I find that on practically every implement the price increased. The price of a 6-foot binder with bundle carrier in 1921 was $235; in 1930 it cost $239, an increase of $4, in spite of the loss suffered by the revenue on sales tax and the lowering of the tariff by 6 per cent. On a six-foot binder the cost in 1921 was $252; the cost in 1930, to the eastern farmer, was $254. For a seven-foot binder the similar figures are $258 and $260; for an eight-foot binder, which cost $266 in 1921, the price in 1930 was $288. That applies to practically every implement item all the way down the line. I am not going to hold up the committee by repeating the entire list. But might I point out what did happen when the tariffs were reduced prior to 1930 as far as importations are concerned. My hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Wood) is not as much concerned or, I think, seriously concerned. In all fairness to him I might recall to him

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
what the hon. member for Brantford city (Mr. Macdonald) is fully aware of, knowing as he does what the industry can do for the people in the city as well as in the surrounding county of Brant. In 1925 we imported into Canada about 86,000,000 of agricultural implements. It is all very well to consider the prices from 1921 to 1930, or 1914 and1 1936 if you will-I realize that the Minister of Agriculture regards that as rather a spectacular comparison. But consider the price of automobiles. As the hon. member for Brantford says, consider the improvement in implements. I know, as one who has purchased binders, that a binder produced in 1930 contains practically double the weight of material which was used in the binder of 1914. The minister referred to cream separators; he knows very well that the cream separator of 1914 and the cream separator of 1935 are two entirely different types; the latter has ball-bearings, timken roller fittings and all the improvements that are placed upon a separator nowadays. It is the fact that just as soon as the tariff was lowered, despite the fact that the sales tax on Canadian implements was removed, we started to import in increasing quantities-in 1925,
56.000.	000 worth; in 1926, 813,000,000 worth; in 1927, 818,000,000 worth, and in 1928,
820.000.	000 worth. In the calendar year 1928 -I want the committee to keep this in mind, and I know the hon. member for Brantford is concerned because of this tendency-we imported into Canada $39,000,000 worth of agricultural implements from the United States.
It is evidence of prosperity.

Any implement
manufacturers can tell you, and they will tell you at this investigation, despite the fact that some believe they are monopolistic concerns-for they have shown us in black and white-that the manufacture of implements involves about 65 per cent labour. I am not going into a long calculation, but I leave it to the committee to say what 65 per cent of 839,000,000 means to the homes in Brantford city, to the home makers of Brant county, and to producers generally.
I should like to ask how Canadian production was as compared with 1924.
That is a fair question. The production did increase substantially. That is very true.
For export purposes.

In all fairness I
would point out as well that in 1911, long before the change in the tariff, and in 1914, before the question of war prices entered into the matter-and that is another factor to which we have not given very much credit for what effect it might have had-we were producing in Canada between sixty and seventy per cent of our consumption. The largest companies manufacturing farm implements in Canada produced seventy per cent of our total consumption in 1911. In order to show the tendency down through the years, in the year during which we imported $39,000,000 worth of agricultural implements we produced only about forty-eight per cent of our consumption.

Was that not due to the
fact that the farmers were buying more tractors, which were put on the free list by the particular school of thought to which the hon. gentleman belongs?

That may have
been one factor.

I think tractors made up
about sixty per cent of those imports.

As I have shown,
since 1925, when the tariff was reduced by six per cent, there has been a gradual increase in our exports, which have risen from
86,000,000 to 839,000,000. I realize that there is a difference in policy as between the two great parties. Something has been said of the brick for brick policy, and I have been misconstrued a couple of times by the Prime Minister in reference to my attitude towards that policy. Certainly I do not want a one way traffic, but in these items generally I think we should be careful not to give the-United States two bricks for every one they give us. I do not think this item affects the Canadian producer very much, because we have never been able to export any large amount to the United States, and it is not likely that we shall do so now.

I should like to ask just one question before this item carries. The other night the hon. gentleman was kind enough to want me to move an amendment to the relevant item in the other schedule, and he wanted to know where I stood. I told him that I stood for taking the tariff entirely off agricultural implements. The hon. gentleman has done a good deal of talking in connection with this item. I want to know whether he agrees with the 12) per cent tariff now in effect, whether he stands for free entry of agricultural imple-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
merits and whether his party was right or wrong in imposing a duty of 25 per cent on agricultural implements.
Is the hon. member asking me a question?
Yes; I am asking if the hon. gentleman supports a 25 per cent duty on agricultural implements, a 12J per cent duty as it is under this agreement, or free entry.

I may say to the
hon. member that while he said he thought of moving an amendment-

I said that the
hon. gentleman asked me to do so.

The hon. member for Moose Jaw said that he was in favour of absolutely free entry for farm implements. I know he will not move any amendment in that connection; he will not embarrass his government in that way. I venture to suggest that only a very small percentage of his party would be in favour of wiping out the tariff, and I do not think that percentage would include the Minister of Finance. I am not so much concerned with whether the duty is 12^ per cent or 25 per cent. I only repeat what has been put on Hansard a score of times since 1925, and what I am sure is the opinion of all intelligent farmers of this country, that raising tariffs does not automatically raise prices. I am reminded again to-day of what was said by a former colleague of the minister's, the late genial Mr. Malcolm, when the duty on furniture was being considered; I expect the Minister of Trade and Commerce will whisper to the Minister of Finance, when he is bringing down his budget, "Do you remember what my genial friend Jim said, that when you raise tariffs you cheapen the cost of production at home because you give the producer a greater or wider market for his own product?" That genial gentleman, a former colleague of the minister, went on record very often as believing that when you raise tariffs you give producers bigger markets at home and thereby reduce the cost of production. I am sure the hon. member for Waterloo North remembers that very well, and I know he could say the same thing.
Do not go away from the subject; what do you say?

I am in agreement with the protectionists of the Liberal party, such as the late Mr. Malcolm and the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is certainly in favour of a reasonable protective

policy because of the benefits that accrue to thousands and thousands of workmen.
I would very much prefer it if the hon. gentleman did not put words into my mouth. I have not said anything like that.

I certainly would not want to put any words into the mouth of my hon. friend, because I know of no protectionist in the house who has been more careful to say nothing with regard to this question. I may tell my hon. friend, however, that I am not so much concerned with whether the rate is 12J per cent, 131 per cent, 241 per cent, or whatever it may be. I believe in a protective policy that will give employment to the workmen of Brantford and so create the best market for the farmers of Brant county. I do not care very much what the protection is as long as it will effect that purpose, without increasing prices to the consumer, and any tariff increases we have had in the past have not raised prices to the consumer. Here we have the spectacle of a member who supports the government presenting a motion for the appointment of a committee to investigate the farm implement industry because prices have gone up since this government has been elected to power.
As a farmer and a purchaser, I am not ashamed to take a stand for the protection of farm implements or anything else that will give employment to Canadians so that they may buy the products of our home producers. I believe there never was a time in the history of this dominion when that policy was more fundamental than it is to-day, when we have thousands standing at the gates of the factories of this dominion looking for work. I say that we shall soon find ourselves on the verge of bankruptcy if we continue to encourage unfavourable trade balances by buying the higher priced, imported, finished article of foreign producers. As a purchaser of farm implements I am satisfied to carry on, having confidence in the manufacturers of Canada, instead of handing over the farmers of thi9 country to the monopolistic control of the manufacturers of any foreign country.

My hon. friend has skated around a good deal of ice, and thin ice at that, in the last few moments. I asked if he were in favour of a 12J per cent duty on farm implements coming into Canada, or of no duty on implements or of a duty of 25 per cent.

Are we discussing implements coming into Canada or implements going into the United States?

speechtext: This item covers implements going out of Canada.

Before this item passes I want to mention one point, particularly to my hon. friends immediately to my left. They say that increasing the tariff increases the volume of production of manufactured goods. I want to direct a question to my hon. friends. Supposing by some misfortune the Conservative party had come into power in 1926 and had raised the tariff as sharply as they raised it in 1930. All these other implements would not have come into the country; the great movement of commodities into Canada between 1926 and 1930 would not have occurred. Their claim is that these goods would have been manufactured in Canada, and in that case production would have reached a tremendous peak. But we know that they had no power to stop the crash when they were in power and had full control. We know that the tariff, high as it was, could not stop the decline in business and could not halt the growth of unemployment in Canada. If there had been a protective tariff from 1926 to 1930; if we had made all the implements they say we would have made; if we had raised the bars against imports, what would have happened to this country when the crash came? As high as we had mounted in delight, in our dejection would we have sunk as low. What does the hon. member for Brantford City want? Does he want employment? Well, there are two methods of having it, the Liberal way and the Conservative way. Between 1930 and 1935 we had the Conservative way, and what did we have? We had the Liberal way between 1926 and 1930, and what did we have? I say to the hon. member for Brantford City-
Is this a debate on the item?

-will he name one year in which we had prosperity when there have been restrictions on imports? Will he name one year in which we have had increased imports without increased prosperity? These observations apply directly to the manufacturing of agricultural implements. Does he wish to shut the door against the prosperity of the farmer, and does he hope that the industrial city of Brantford can rise triumphant on a degraded agriculture? It cannot be done.
The Massey Harris Company were good enough to send me their prices showing the difference between 1913 and 1936. Those prices have gone up 61 per cent. I ask this
question not in a partisan way, but as a business problem: Can the farmers buy implements when prices of agricultural implements have increased by 61 per cent while prices of farm produce have remained exactly where they were? I ask the same question of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe and of every Canadian manufacturer:	Can we
expand the manufacturing industries of Canada while there is a wide hiatus between these two price levels? That is the problem I place before the committee. I appeal to the committee in a non-partisan way, if it is possible for me to do so. I appeal to the hon. member in an open and non-partisan way; possibly he can rise to a higher level than I can in the matter. There is a great gap between prices of manufactured goods and those of farm products. Does the manufacturer wish to maintain that gap? Does he seriously contend that raising prices through raising duties will have the effect of lowering the price to the consumer? If he does, then let him come forward and say so. If he thinks that raising the duty will have the effect of lowering the price, let him tell us why it is that the Canadian Manufacturers Association is out for a high tariff.
Is it?

What is its record?
I offer to the hon. member the challenge which he offered a few days ago. Let the Canadian Manufacturers Association come out and announce to Canada that henceforward its policy is one of an increase in tariffs on raw materials. Let every lobbyist who has come here asking for a reduction in duty upon his raw material come forward and say, "Raise the duty upon my raw material, in order that the price may be brought down."

You know better
than that.
And so do you. That is the challenge.

Would the hon.
member-

I have only a minute more to speak. I ask that the committee consider the problem seriously, not only as it applies to agricultural implements, but as it applies to the spread between the price levels of farm products and manufactured products. Do we wish to maintain that price level, or do we wish to bring about conditions whereby the two would be upon a uniform level, thereby restoring equilibrium in price structure? If lowering the tariff is not the
